resources.string: LSPosed virtual location — spoof GPS without enabling mock locations
Why is the module not active?

FakeLoc reads and writes its configuration through a service that LSPosed binds. Three things stop it working:

1. The module is not enabled in LSPosed.
2. It is enabled, but this app was opened before that happened — force-stop this app, then reopen it.
3. The target app is not in scope, or it sits in Magisk's DenyList. DenyList stops every module from loading into an app, this one included.

After changing the scope, restart the target app: a policy change does not reach a process that is already running.
Enable FakeLoc in LSPosed, force-stop this app, then reopen it. The module talks to LSPosed over its bound service.

Off: no accuracy is sent, so the SDK answers with the value it computed itself.
Off: no altitude is sent, so the SDK answers with the real terrain height of where the phone actually is.
Off: no speed is sent, so the SDK derives it from the distance between consecutive fixes.
Off: the coordinates are one frozen point, and the track shows no movement at all — which, for an account that usually moves, is the more suspicious of the two.
Neutralises isFromMockProvider/isMock, the mock_location setting and the AppOps check, so detectors see nothing.
Denies WiFi scans, cell information and raw GNSS (NMEA, measurements). Without those inputs an app cannot compute a real fix of its own and fall back to it.
Hooks the Tencent location SDK directly — including the instances the app loads on its own. Needed for apps that read their position from a map SDK instead of the system.

Answers the city, province, district and address getters of the map SDK with the values the map picker resolved for the anchor. Apps that display the city a location SDK reports need this: a real or empty address keeps them showing where you really are. Turn it off if an app misbehaves.

Currently a custom combination — no scene preset matches.
Altitude does not follow the scene: the plausible value depends on the terrain of the city you picked, so any number baked in here would be wrong elsewhere.
All four are on by default; they are what keeps a forged position from being spotted, and turning one off is a repair step, not a setting.
Off: isFromMockProvider / isMock report the truth again, and a basic check gives the fix away.
Off: the app can recompute a real position from WiFi scans and cell towers — the map jumps to the fake point and drifts back seconds later.
Off: only the system location is rewritten. An app that reads its fix from the Tencent SDK still gets real coordinates, while this page keeps showing the fake ones.
Off: province, city, district and address come from the real fix again — the map is already at the fake point while the header names your real city.

The module will only rewrite the system location. Apps that read their position from a Tencent SDK — banking, check-in, delivery — get your real coordinates while the home screen keeps showing the fake ones. It looks like the module stopped working; it did.
Coordinates stay fake, but province, city, district and address revert to the real ones — a fake map with a real city in the header, easier to notice than a wholly fake position.
A forged position is a set of numbers, and accuracy, speed and drift have to agree with each other. Pick a scene first, refine if none fits — every change is written to the config as you make it.
Affects only the picker’s base map and address lookup; the module itself needs no key.

The picker draws with Tencent’s base map, and looks addresses up through the system geocoder. The module itself forges positions and needs no map key at all — this page only affects the “pick on a map” screen.
This build ships no key of its own — paste your own Tencent key.
Key present — run the test below to see whether Tencent accepts it.
No key yet; the picker will show an empty map until you add one.
Needed only when that key has key signing switched on: without the matching secret, Tencent rejects every request with status 111. Leave blank otherwise.
No answer — check the network connection, then try again.
Status 111 · signature rejected. Fill in the SK below, or switch key signing off for this key in the console.
Status 112 · the request origin is not allowed. Empty the IP whitelist for this key, or add one that matches.
Status 113 · this interface has no quota. Assign one under 配额管理 in the console — it is a separate step from enabling the product.
Status 199 · WebServiceAPI is not enabled for this key. Tick it under the key\'s enabled products.
Status 120 · the daily call quota for this key is used up.
Status 190 · the key is not valid. Check for a character that came along when pasting.
Status %1$d · not a code this build knows. See the status table in Tencent\'s documentation.
A key change takes effect after this app is restarted: the SDK reads its key once, at launch.
What the console will ask for
The key is bound to this package name and this certificate — one character off and it is rejected, with an error that looks like a wrong key. Copy, do not retype.
Getting a key and its quota
Four separate gates for %1$s: the key itself, its signing secret, the endpoint quota, and the call source. Skip any one and the key looks valid while doing nothing. Open the steps below.

1. Sign in at lbs.qq.com → Console → Application management → My applications → Create application (a mere container, any name) → Add key.
2. Enable two products on that one key: Android SDK (basemap) and WebService API (reverse geocoding, keyword lookup). Separate entitlements — with Android SDK alone the map draws and the address never resolves.
3. Android SDK requires a package name and SHA-1: enter %1$s, and copy the SHA-1 from "The two values the console asks for" above.
4. The whole string shown on the key's row after saving is the key; copy it into Tencent Maps key above.
2 · Get the SK (signing secret) — only if signing is on

1. My applications → the key → Settings; check the signature verification switch.\n2. Off → leave the SK blank. On → copy the 32-character signature secret shown on the same page into Tencent signing secret (SK) above.\n3. With signing on but the SK missing or wrong, every request returns status 111 — the most common reason a valid key never resolves an address.
3 · Assign endpoint quota (the step everyone misses)

1. Console → Quota management; find WebService API → Reverse geocoding and set the daily volume above zero (1000 calls/day is plenty for testing).\n2. Quota is allocated per endpoint: an allowance for keyword lookup does not cover reverse geocoding; add whichever is missing.\n3. Enabling the product without quota returns status 113; a reply of 112 / 110 means the call-source allow-list blocked the request — clear it (the app sends no Referer).

0 — success
111 — signature rejected → fill the SK, or turn signing off
112 / 110 — call source not allowed → clear the allow-list
113 — this endpoint has no quota → assign it under Quota management
199 — WebService API not enabled → back to step 1
190 / 120 — invalid key / daily limit reached
Keys stay on this device, in the module’s own preferences, and are sent only to the platform’s own servers by that platform’s SDK.
